title: Main Memory, Virtual Memory and TLB
subtitle: From DRAM chips to the address translation every access goes through.

references.title: Large and Fast: Exploiting Memory Hierarchy
references.topics: Memory technologies (SRAM, DRAM); virtual memory: pages, page tables, page faults, the TLB, protection

objectives: Compare SRAM and DRAM and explain where each is used
Distinguish memory latency from bandwidth and calculate both
Translate a virtual address into a physical address using a page table
Follow the path virtual address, TLB, page table, physical address, RAM
Explain page faults, demand paging and protection

steps.question: Every program believes it owns the whole memory starting at address 0. How can ten programs all think that at the same time?
clues: Programs use **virtual addresses** that the hardware translates.
Each program has its own **page table**.
A small cache called the **TLB** makes the translation fast.

notes.explain: Let students guess before revealing the clues.
Read the objectives aloud; they return in the learning report.

steps.title: SRAM and DRAM

head: SRAM
DRAM
rows: Needed: the charge leaks away and is periodically rewritten

steps.why: This difference is why the hierarchy has fast small caches (SRAM) and slow large main memory (DRAM).
steps.real: Main memory is a bank of DRAM chips on modules; caches are SRAM on the processor die.

mistake.wrong: DRAM is faster because it is newer.
mistake.right: DRAM is slower than SRAM; its advantage is density and cost per bit.

explainAgain.beginner: SRAM is a notepad that keeps what you write; DRAM is a chalkboard that fades unless you keep rewriting it, but one board holds far more.

steps.title: Latency and bandwidth

head: Term
Meaning
Typical
rows: Time from a request until the first data arrives
Data transferred per second once flowing
tens of GB/s per memory channel

terms.t: bandwidth = transfers per second × bytes per transfer
terms.note: a DDR4-3200 module does 3.2 billion 8-byte transfers per second = 25.6 GB/s

terms.t: time for a block = latency + block size ÷ bandwidth

steps.why: A cache miss pays the latency once and then streams the block at the memory bandwidth.
steps.real: Wide memory buses and several channels raise bandwidth, but latency has improved little.

deeper.text: DRAM is organised in rows and columns; reading a row that is already open (a row hit) is faster than opening a new row.

steps.title: Calculate: latency and bandwidth

blocks.title: Fetching a cache block from DRAM (illustrative)

steps.why: With the defaults: 25.6 GB/s, 2.5 ns of transfer, 52.5 ns in all. The latency is 95% of the time: a faster bus alone barely changes it.

steps.question: DRAM latency 50 ns, bandwidth 25.6 GB/s. How long does it take to fetch a 64-byte block?

reveal.text: The transfer takes 64 ÷ 25.6 = 2.5 ns after the 50 ns latency: **52.5 ns**.

steps.result: Latency dominates for a single small block.

steps.title: Mini challenge
steps.prompt: Match each term with its meaning.

pairs.b: Fast, expensive memory used for caches
Dense, cheap memory that needs refresh
Time until the first data arrives

steps.why: These four terms are the vocabulary of main memory.

steps.question: Why does DRAM need refreshing?
options: It is read destructively by the CPU only
steps.why: The charge in a DRAM capacitor leaks away, so the cells are rewritten periodically.
feedback: Refresh is needed even when idle.

steps.title: Why virtual addresses?

items: Each program sees its own **virtual address space** starting at 0
The hardware and OS map **virtual pages** to **physical frames** in main memory
Many programs can run at once without overwriting each other
A program can be larger than physical memory: pages not in use stay on disk
The operating system can place pages anywhere, so memory need not be contiguous

steps.why: Virtual memory gives protection, convenience and the illusion of a large, private memory.
steps.real: Every modern operating system uses it; a process cannot read another process's memory.

mistake.wrong: A virtual address is a location in RAM.
mistake.right: It is a name that must be translated into a physical address first.

explainAgain.beginner: A hotel: your room number "101" means a different physical room on each floor of different hotels. The reception desk (the page table) knows which one is yours.

steps.title: Pages, frames and the page table

head: Term
Meaning
rows: A fixed-size block of virtual memory (commonly 4 KiB)
A page-sized slot in physical memory
Per-process table mapping VPN to frame number, with a valid bit

terms.note: 4 KiB: 12 bits; the offset is not translated

terms.t: physical address = frame number × page size + offset
terms.note: the VPN is replaced by the frame number

steps.why: Only the page number is translated; the offset inside the page is copied unchanged.
steps.real: A 32-bit address with 4 KiB pages has a 20-bit page number and a 12-bit offset.

steps.title: Try it: translate an address

blocks.title: Virtual to physical

inputs.label: Frame number from the page table

stages.label: Split
stages.text: VPN = **{floor(va / pow(2, pb))}**, offset = **{mod(va, pow(2, pb))}**

stages.label: Page table
stages.text: Page {floor(va / pow(2, pb))} is in frame **{ppn}** (valid)

stages.label: Physical address
stages.text: {ppn} × {pow(2, pb)} + {mod(va, pow(2, pb))} = **{ppn * pow(2, pb) + mod(va, pow(2, pb))}** (`{ppn * pow(2, pb) + mod(va, pow(2, pb))|hex4}`)

blocks.result: VA {va} → PA {ppn * pow(2, pb) + mod(va, pow(2, pb))}
blocks.note: With 4 KiB pages, address 5000 is page 1, offset 904; if page 1 is in frame 7 the physical address is 7 × 4096 + 904 = 29,576.

steps.why: Change the page size and see the VPN and offset change; the physical address always keeps the same offset.

steps.question: 4 KiB pages. Virtual address 5000 is in page 1 and page 1 is stored in frame 7. What is the physical address?

steps.title: Calculate: how big is a page table?
steps.why: 32-bit addresses, 4 KiB pages, 4-byte entries: 2^20 entries = 4 MiB per process. With 16 KiB pages it is 1 MiB. This is why real systems use multi-level page tables.

steps.title: Find the mistake
steps.prompt: One statement about paging is wrong. Click it.
lines: 1. The page offset is the same in the virtual and the physical address.
2. The page table maps virtual page numbers to physical frames.
3. Each process normally has its own page table.
4. The whole virtual address is replaced by the frame number.
steps.explain: Only the virtual page number is replaced; the offset is kept.

steps.title: The translation problem

items: The page table lives in **main memory**, so a translation would cost an extra memory access on **every** load and store
The **translation lookaside buffer (TLB)** is a small cache of recent translations (VPN to frame)
TLB hit: translation in about one cycle. TLB miss: read the page table, then update the TLB
The TLB works because of **locality**: successive accesses fall in the same few pages

steps.why: Without a TLB every memory access would take about twice as long.
steps.real: A typical TLB has 32 to 1024 entries and hits over 99% of the time.

steps.title: The path of an address

blocks.text: Follow the whole journey of an address through the hardware.

steps.why: This is the path to remember: Virtual address → TLB → page table → physical address → RAM.

steps.title: Build the path

steps.text: The program uses a **virtual address**. The first stop is the **TLB**, a small cache of recent translations.
On a **TLB hit** the frame number is available at once: it is combined with the offset into a **physical address** and sent to main memory.
On a **TLB miss** the **page table** in memory is consulted. If the page is in memory its entry gives the frame number, and the TLB is updated.
If the entry is invalid the page is not in memory: a **page fault**. The operating system loads the page from disk.

steps.why: Each click adds one component. The page table is only visited on a TLB miss.

steps.title: Follow three accesses

steps.text: The complete path. Choose a scenario and press Play or Step.
The CPU sends virtual address 4200 (page 1, offset 104). The TLB already holds page 1.
The frame number is combined with the offset: 0 × 4096 + 104.
Main memory is accessed at physical address 104. No page table access was needed.
Virtual address 100 (page 0). The TLB does not have it.
The page table is read from memory: page 0 is valid and lives in frame 2.
Physical address = 2 × 4096 + 100 = 8292. The TLB is updated with this translation.
The page table entry for page 1 is **invalid**: the page is not in memory.
**Page fault.** The operating system reads the page from disk (millions of cycles), picks a free frame (or evicts one), updates the page table and the TLB, and restarts the instruction.
The retried access now succeeds: page 1 is in frame 0, so the physical address is 904.

steps.why: Run the TLB hit, the TLB miss with the page in memory, and the page fault.

steps.title: Page faults and demand paging

items: A page table entry is **invalid** when the page is not in physical memory
The access causes a **page fault**: an exception handled by the operating system
**Demand paging**: pages are brought in only when first used
The OS picks a free frame (or evicts one, usually the least recently used), reads the page from **disk**, updates the page table and TLB, and restarts the instruction
A disk access takes millions of cycles, so page faults must be rare

head: Event
Cost (about)
rows: tens to hundreds of cycles (page table read)

steps.why: A page fault is thousands of times costlier than a memory access, so even a tiny fault rate matters.
steps.real: When a computer starts using the disk heavily because it lacks memory it is "thrashing".

mistake.wrong: A page fault means the program has a bug.
mistake.right: It is a normal event: the page was simply not in memory yet.

steps.title: Try it: a sequence of accesses

blocks.title: Address translation
blocks.hint: Step through the six addresses. Page size 4 KiB, a 2-entry TLB, 3 frames. Page 0 starts in frame 2.

steps.why: Results: 100 = TLB miss but page valid (frame 2), 5000 = page fault (frame 0), 4200 = TLB hit, 9000 = page fault, 13000 = page fault that evicts page 0, and 100 again = a fault because page 0 was evicted.

steps.question: In the sequence above, address 4200 follows 5000. Why is it a TLB hit?
options: Both are in virtual page 1, whose translation was just stored in the TLB

reveal.text: 5000 and 4200 are both in page 1 (4096 to 8191). The page fault for 5000 loaded page 1 and put its translation in the TLB, so 4200 hits: **locality again**.

steps.result: Next access to a different page needs a new translation.

steps.title: Calculate: effective access time

blocks.title: Effective access time with a TLB (illustrative)
blocks.equation: EAT = hit rate × (TLB + memory) + miss rate × (TLB + 2 × memory)

results.label: Compared with no TLB (2 memory accesses)

steps.why: A 98% TLB hit rate gives 103 ns, close to the single memory access time; without a TLB every access would take about 200 ns.

steps.title: Think, pair, share
steps.prompt: Why is a TLB with only 64 entries so effective when the page table has a million entries?
steps.answer: Programs use only a small set of pages at a time (locality): a loop touches a few code pages and a few data pages. 64 entries cover the working set of pages, so almost every translation hits in the TLB.

questions.a: Recent translations from virtual page number to frame number.

questions.q: What happens on a page fault?
questions.a: The OS loads the page from disk, updates the page table and TLB, and restarts the instruction.

questions.q: Give the path of an address.
questions.a: Virtual address, TLB, page table (on a miss), physical address, RAM.

steps.title: Protection and sharing

items: Each process has its **own page table**, so it can only reach the frames the OS maps for it
Page table entries also hold **permission bits** (read, write, execute) and **dirty** and **reference** bits
A forbidden access causes an exception and the OS stops the program (a segmentation fault)
Two processes can share a library by mapping the **same frame** into both address spaces
The OS alone can change page tables: the hardware enforces user / kernel modes

steps.why: The same mechanism that makes memory look big and private also keeps programs apart.
steps.real: This is how a crashing program cannot corrupt another program or the operating system.

steps.title: The cost of page faults

blocks.title: Effective access time with page faults (illustrative)
blocks.equation: EAT = memory time + fault rate × disk time

steps.why: One fault per million accesses already raises 100 ns to 108 ns. At one fault per thousand accesses (1,000 per million) it becomes 8,100 ns: 81 times slower.

steps.question: One page fault per million memory accesses, memory 100 ns, fault service 8 ms (8,000,000 ns). What is the effective access time?
steps.result: At 1 fault per 1000 accesses it would be 8,100 ns.

steps.title: Discussion
steps.question: Why do operating systems use virtual memory even on machines with plenty of RAM?
ideas: Protection: processes cannot read each other's memory.
Convenience: each program has a simple, private address space.
Sharing: libraries can be mapped into many processes with one copy.
Flexibility: the OS can move or swap pages freely.

steps.statement: Two processes may map the same physical frame into their address spaces.
steps.why: This is how shared libraries and shared memory are implemented.

steps.question: Where does the OS keep each process's mapping from virtual pages to frames?
steps.why: Each process has its own page table; the TLB caches recent entries.
feedback: The TLB is only a cache of the page table.
The page table is in main memory.

steps.question: Define virtual address and physical address.
steps.answer: A virtual address is the address used by the program; a physical address is the location in main memory after translation.
steps.solution: The page table (and TLB) performs the translation.

steps.question: 4 KiB pages. Split virtual address 0x3A7C into page number and offset.
steps.solution: 0x3A7C = 14,972. 14,972 ÷ 4096 = 3 remainder 2,684. The low 12 bits (0xA7C) are the offset.
steps.hint: The offset is the low 12 bits.

steps.question: 4 KiB pages, page 1 in frame 7. What is the physical address of virtual address 5000?
steps.hint: Keep the offset and swap the page number for the frame number.

steps.question: 32-bit virtual addresses, 4 KiB pages, 4-byte page table entries. Give the VPN and offset bits, the number of entries and the page table size. Repeat for 16 KiB pages.
steps.answer: 4 KiB: 20 + 12 bits, 2^20 entries, 4 MiB. 16 KiB: 18 + 14 bits, 2^18 entries, 1 MiB.
steps.solution: Offset = log2(page size). VPN = 32 − offset. Size = entries × 4 bytes: 2^20 × 4 = 4 MiB; 2^18 × 4 = 1 MiB.
steps.mistake: Counting the offset bits in the page table index.
steps.title: Exam practice: sizes

steps.question: 4 KiB pages, a 2-entry TLB, 3 frames. Page 0 starts valid in frame 2. Translate 100, 5000, 4200, 9000, 13000, 100. Give hit / miss / fault for each and the physical addresses of the first three.
steps.answer: 100: TLB miss, page valid, PA 8,292. 5000: page fault, frame 0, PA 904. 4200: TLB hit, PA 104. 9000: page fault (frame 1). 13000: page fault, evicts page 0. 100: page fault (page 0 was evicted).
steps.solution: Page numbers: 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 0. Only three frames, so loading page 3 forces an eviction of the least recently used page, which is page 0.
steps.mistake: Treating the first 100 as a TLB hit: the TLB starts empty.
steps.title: Exam practice: tracing

steps.question: TLB lookup 1 ns, memory 100 ns, TLB hit rate 98%. A TLB miss needs one extra memory access. Find the effective access time.
steps.mistake: Forgetting the final data access on a miss.
steps.title: Exam practice: effective access time

steps.question: Memory takes 100 ns and a page fault takes 8 ms. What page-fault rate raises the effective access time by 10%?
steps.mistake: Using the hit rate instead of the fault rate.
steps.title: Exam practice: page faults

steps.question: Explain why the TLB is needed and why it works.
steps.answer: The page table is in main memory, so without a TLB every load and store would need an extra memory access for the translation. The TLB caches recent translations; because programs show locality and keep using the same few pages, almost every translation hits in the TLB and costs about one cycle.
steps.solution: A strong answer states the extra memory access and the locality argument.
steps.title: Exam practice: conceptual
What you should remember
remember: SRAM is fast and costly (caches); DRAM is dense and cheap but needs refresh (main memory).
Latency is time to the first data; bandwidth is bytes per second. Block time = latency + size ÷ bandwidth.
A virtual address = page number + offset; the page table maps pages to frames; the offset is unchanged.
The TLB caches translations: virtual address, TLB, page table (on a miss), physical address, RAM.
A page fault is an invalid page table entry: the OS loads the page from disk (demand paging).
Protection comes from per-process page tables and permission bits.

mistakes.wrong: A virtual address is a location in RAM.

mistakes.right: They are normal but must be infrequent because disk is slow.

steps.title: One-minute summary
steps.summary: DRAM gives large, cheap main memory while SRAM provides fast caches. Programs use virtual addresses split into a page number and an offset; the page table maps pages to physical frames and the TLB caches recent translations. A page fault brings a page from disk on demand, and per-process page tables with permission bits provide protection.
